We combine the sum and the constant multiple rules, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (g(x)+\sqrt{h(x)})\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{2}+4x+1+\sqrt{{e}^{2x}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2{x}^{2}+4x+1+{e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & =2\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+4\int x\,\text{d}x+\int \,\text{d}x+\int {e}^{x}\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+4\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+x+{e}^{x}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}+2{x}^{2}+x+{e}^{x}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

We combine the sum and the constant multiple rules, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (g(x)+\sqrt{h(x)})\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{2}+4x+1+\sqrt{{e}^{2x}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2{x}^{2}+4x+1+{e}^{x})\text{d}x \\  & =2\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+4\int x\,\text{d}x+\int \,\text{d}x+\int {e}^{x}\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+4\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+x+{e}^{x}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}+2{x}^{2}+x+{e}^{x}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

We know that 

$$
\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,\,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Applying these formulae and the constant multiple rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+3\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =2(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+3(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

In part 2, we found that

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the second derivative, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-3\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =2(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-3(\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate using the product rule. 

In part 2 we found that $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =x\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}+f\frac{\text{d}(x)}{\text{d}x} \\  & =x\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot 1 \\  & =(2-3x)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+(3+2x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=0$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & =(2-3(0))\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+(3+2(0))\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $3.$

feedback.worked_solution:
When $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =0\cdot f(0)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

In part 3, we found that the slope of the tangent line to the curve $y=x\cdot f(x)$ at the point where $x=0$ is $m=3.$ Therefore, the slope of the normal ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-0) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $f(x)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$

We apply the quotient rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{f}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}) & =\frac{{f}^{′}(x)\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-f(x)\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡x-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}-3{sin}^{2}⁡x\cancel{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-3{cos}^{2}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{-3({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{3}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $y$ is a composite function:

$$
y={e}^{s},\,s=2g=2(2{x}^{2}+4x+1)=4{x}^{2}+8x+2.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}={e}^{s},\,\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}x}=8x+8.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}\cdot \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{s}\cdot (8x+8) \\  & =(8x+8)\,{e}^{4{x}^{2}+8x+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C,\,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int f(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x+3\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.
